summary: Moon2Earth is an interactive web app that can help astronauts explore how Earth can prepare us for future lunar exploration. Users can select a location on an interactive 3D Moon, and the app analyzes its selected tiles using NASA-derived data. It then identifies the best matching Earth analog locations based on shared physical and environmental characteristics. Finally, Moon2Earth generates an explorable 3D terrain environment of the most similar Earth analog, allowing users to walk through the landscape and understand how Earth-based environments can help scientists and engineers prepare for future Moon bases and missions.
details:
Moon2earth is a application that determines the analogs of potential moon bases of Earth, which are locations that are used to simulate the conditions of lunar surface.

Features:
- Both the Earth and Moon separated into thousands of tiles, each of which contain certain data on their features and characteristics

- Every Earth tile has topological, meteorological, geographical, geological and climate data, while Moon tiles stores topological and geological information

- The program compares features from the selected Moon tile with all Earth tiles to determine accurate analogs from around the world

- Pros and cons of each analog location are identified, and locations are ranked by compatibility with the proposed moon base location

Tools:

- Visual Studio Code

- Vite + Vercel

- NASA PDS Geosciences Node Lunar Orbital Data Explorer

- NASA EarthData Topography Datasets

- NASA POWER Data Access Viewer

- OpenTopography + EarthAccess

Languages & Frameworks:
- HTML/CSS

- JavaScript

- React.js + Three.js

Creativity:

- Splits the Earth and Moon into hexagonal sectors inspired by Uber's H3 Hierarchical Spatial Index

- Uses 3D renders of the Moon and Earth rather than maps for an accurate visualization, and saves the positions of past landing sites

- Uses a unique weighting algorithm to determine analogs to locations on the Moon, based on terrain compatibility, weather, average slope, and surface roughness

Factors Considered:

- It would be too hardware intensive and restricted to get data for every single distinct location on Earth, so we decided to chunk the Earth into hexagonal tiles, which share similar characteristics

- Certain data such as the locations of caves and geological formations would be too difficult to discover and compare, so we decided to focus on area-wide data collected by satellites and weather stations
